name: KN-23 short-range ballistic missile
operator: Korean People's Army; supplied to Russia
overview_md:
The KN-23 is North Korea's solid-fuelled short-range ballistic missile — a weapon closely resembling Russia's Iskander and built to do the one thing that most troubles regional missile defences: manoeuvre. First flown in 2019, it has become the workhorse of Pyongyang's expanding theatre missile force, threatening targets across South Korea and reaching into Japan.

Its danger lies in its trajectory. Rather than following the predictable arc of a classic ballistic missile, the KN-23 flies a depressed, quasi-ballistic path and performs "pull-up" manoeuvres in its terminal phase, which complicates tracking and interception by systems like Patriot and the indigenous Cheongung. It is solid-fuelled — so it can launch quickly with little warning — road-mobile, and has been tested from rail cars and even reservoirs, all to improve survivability and unpredictability. Variants carry large conventional warheads, and a nuclear role is assessed.

For an analyst, the KN-23 is doubly significant. Regionally, it is the precision theatre weapon that could strike South Korean and U.S. bases, command nodes and ports in the opening minutes of a war. Globally, North Korea has supplied large numbers of KN-23s to Russia for use against Ukraine, providing a real-world combat record — and Pyongyang invaluable feedback — while deepening the Moscow–Pyongyang axis that increasingly shapes Indo-Pacific security.

additional.trajectory: Depressed quasi-ballistic with terminal pull-up manoeuvre

variants_json.name: KN-23 extended / 'super-large' family
variants_json.key_changes: Longer range and larger warhead variants

combat_history.event: KN-23 missiles supplied by North Korea were used by Russia against Ukraine.
combat_history.significance: Provided a real combat record and feedback, and deepened the Russia–DPRK arms relationship.

combat_history.event: Repeatedly flight-tested, including manoeuvring and low-apogee profiles.
combat_history.significance: Demonstrated a missile designed to defeat regional missile defences.

modernization.description: Longer-range and larger-warhead variants; diversified launch modes.
modernization.impact: Broadens the theatre threat and improves survivability.

vulnerabilities.description: Real-world precision is debated; combat use in Ukraine showed mixed results.
vulnerabilities.context: Claimed precision not always borne out.

vulnerabilities.description: Manoeuvring is hard but not impossible to intercept for modern hit-to-kill SAMs.

operational_patterns.typical_deployment: Road-mobile theatre strikes against South Korean and U.S. bases, ports and command nodes; exported to Russia.
operational_patterns.typical_task_group: KPA missile units; mobile dispersed launchers.

peer_comparisons.key_differences: The KN-23 closely resembles the Russian Iskander in its manoeuvring quasi-ballistic profile.
South Korean precision missiles built to strike back at North Korean launchers.
peer_comparisons.video_angle: The missile duel on the Korean Peninsula.

peer_comparisons.key_differences: The Hwasong-17 is the intercontinental tier; the KN-23 is the manoeuvring theatre weapon.

doctrine.role: Solid-fuel manoeuvring short-range ballistic missile for precision theatre strikes that defeat missile defences.
doctrine.employment: Rapid road-mobile launch on a depressed, manoeuvring trajectory against bases and command nodes.
doctrine.design_philosophy: Manoeuvre and quick launch to defeat defences and minimise warning.
doctrine.threat_context: Threatens South Korea and Japan and, supplied to Russia, has a real combat record against Ukraine.
doctrine.comparison_frame: Read against the Russian Iskander, South Korea's Hyunmoo and the Hwasong-17.
